# cdtr

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/hypertidy/cdtr/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/hypertidy/cdtr/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

Constrained Delaunay triangulation with refinement for R, binding the
header-only [CDT](https://github.com/artem-ogre/CDT) library (MPL-2.0). It
takes the same input as a planar straight line graph (vertices, segments as
index pairs, optional per-vertex attributes) and returns vertices, triangles,
and a per-triangle *depth* that says where each triangle sits relative to the
constraints, with no point-in-polygon step.

```r
remotes::install_github("hypertidy/cdtr")
```

## The pipeline, on a toy

Vertices and segments in, vertices and triangles out. Here a square with a
square hole: two closed rings of segments.

```{r toy}
library(cdtr)
x <- c(0, 1, 1, 0, 0.25, 0.75, 0.75, 0.25)
y <- c(0, 0, 1, 1, 0.25, 0.25, 0.75, 0.75)
s0 <- 1:8; s1 <- c(2, 3, 4, 1, 6, 7, 8, 5)
r <- cdt_triangulate(x, y, s0, s1)
str(r[c("P", "T", "S", "depth")])
```

`depth` is the number of constraint boundaries crossed on the way in from
outside: 0 is outside everything, and for nested rings odd is inside, even is
a hole. By default triangles outside the outermost boundary are already
dropped (`erase = "outer"`, which is what Triangle's `-p` does);
`erase = "holes"` also drops the even depths.

```{r toy-plot, fig.height = 3.2}
plot_mesh <- function(m, main = "") {
  e <- cdt_edges(m)
  plot(m$P, asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", pch = ".", main = main)
  segments(m$P[e[, 1], 1], m$P[e[, 1], 2], m$P[e[, 2], 1], m$P[e[, 2], 2], col = "grey50")
  segments(m$P[m$S[, 1], 1], m$P[m$S[, 1], 2], m$P[m$S[, 2], 1], m$P[m$S[, 2], 2], lwd = 2)
}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
plot_mesh(r, "constrained")
plot_mesh(cdt_triangulate(x, y, s0, s1, max_area = 0.01), "max_area = 0.01")
plot_mesh(cdt_triangulate(x, y, s0, s1, max_area = 0.01, min_angle = 25, erase = "holes"),
          "+ min_angle = 25, holes erased")
par(op)
```

## Refinement reports what it could not do

Ruppert refinement cannot always meet the bound (two constraints meeting at a
sharp angle, say). Rather than silently stopping, the result carries the counts.

```{r unrefined}
r2 <- cdt_triangulate(x, y, s0, s1, max_area = 0.01, min_angle = 25)
r2$unrefined
r2$min_edge_length
```

`min_edge_length` is the floor below which the refiner gives up on an edge;
by default it is derived from the input (a fraction of the median segment
length, capped by the area target) so refinement does not cascade into sharp
input corners. Pass `0` for never-give-up.

### Refinement protects the constraints

Refinement follows Ruppert's algorithm: a constraint segment is split whenever
a vertex lies inside the circle on its diameter, and this applies to `max_area`
alone as well as to `min_angle`. So a mesh refined by area has more vertices
along the constraints than one from a refiner that only splits large triangles
(Triangle with `a` but no `q`, for example). With `max_area` set to 1/5000 of
the bounding box area, on North Carolina's counties and anglr's Tasmanian
cadastre and contours, cdtr adds 1.2 to 1.3 times as many Steiner vertices as
Triangle with `a` alone, and 40 to 62% of them lie on the input constraints,
against 11 to 14% of Triangle's. On the two polygon layers that buys shape:
0.1% of cdtr's triangles have a minimum angle under 5 degrees on the counties,
against 0.6% of Triangle's, and 1.7% against 3.0% on the cadastre. On the
contours the share is the same, 1.4%. These figures come from
`inst/benchmarks/bench5.R`.

`min_edge_length` is the control. Edges shorter than it are not split, so a
larger value gives a coarser mesh. By default it is derived from the input (2.8
on the contours, where `sqrt(max_area)` is 12). On these three inputs a floor
of `sqrt(max_area)` cuts cdtr's Steiner vertices by 10 to 12%, and the area
target is still met everywhere on the two polygon layers. Raise it in steps,
and check `unrefined` and the largest triangle area each time.

## Holes as points

`erase = "holes"` drops the even depths. A hole can also be given as a point,
as the `H` of an `RTriangle::pslg()`: the region around it that is bounded by
segments is erased, whatever its depth.

```{r holes}
rh <- cdt_triangulate(x, y, s0, s1, holes = cbind(0.5, 0.5))
table(rh$depth)
```

## Real polygons

Any polygon source reduces to the same two tables. With `sf`'s North Carolina
counties, rings become vertex runs and consecutive index pairs; shared
boundaries dedupe to one segment.

```{r nc, fig.height = 4}
nc <- sf::st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
rings <- unlist(lapply(sf::st_geometry(nc), function(g) lapply(unclass(g), `[[`, 1)), recursive = FALSE)
xy <- do.call(rbind, lapply(rings, function(m) m[-nrow(m), ]))
n <- vapply(rings, function(m) nrow(m) - 1L, 1L)
start <- rep(cumsum(c(0L, n[-length(n)])), n)
s0 <- seq_along(xy[, 1])
s1 <- start + (s0 - start) %% rep(n, n) + 1L
m <- cdt_triangulate(xy[, 1], xy[, 2], s0, s1, max_area = 0.01)
table(m$depth)
op <- par(mar = rep(0, 4))
plot_mesh(m)
par(op)
```

The counties tile the state, so there are no holes, but a county two
boundaries in from the coast has depth 3, and so on: depth is the peel
layer, a count of constraint crossings from outside, not an inside/outside
flag in general. It is computed topologically from the mesh alone, before
anything is erased, which makes it a cheap first cut for classifying
triangles by region: nested rings get odd/even, a coverage gets a
boundary-distance ordering, and only ties within a layer need a geometric
lookup.

## Attributes ride along

Per-vertex values (an elevation, a time) are carried onto the new Steiner
vertices by linear interpolation from the input mesh, the way Triangle's `PA`
works.

```{r attr}
z <- 2 * xy[, 1] + 3 * xy[, 2]
ma <- cdt_triangulate_attr(xy[, 1], xy[, 2], s0, s1, PA = cbind(z = z), max_area = 0.01)
range(ma$PA[, "z"] - (2 * ma$P[, 1] + 3 * ma$P[, 2]))
```

## Mesh quality

`cdt_quality()` gives the shape of every triangle: area, angles, edge lengths
and radius-edge ratio.

```{r quality}
summary(cdt_quality(m)[c("area", "min_angle", "radius_edge")])
```

## Where points fall

`cdt_locate()` finds the triangle holding each query point with exact
orientation tests, so a point on a shared edge is never lost between triangles.
With `barycentric = TRUE` it also gives the weights of the triangle's vertices
at each point.

```{r locate}
cdt_locate(m$P, m$T, c(-80, -79), c(35.5, 35.5), barycentric = TRUE)
```

## Where input came from

`edge_sources = TRUE` returns, for every fixed edge, the input segments that
cover it (through crossings, splits and refinement). That lets regions be
labelled by which inputs cover them, which `depth` cannot do, and
`cdt_winding()` uses it to give the winding number of each input feature in every
triangle, for overlapping polygons, with no point-in-polygon test. See
`vignette("overlay")`.

## Working with polygons: wkpool and polymer

The [wkpool](https://hypertidy.github.io/wkpool/) package (0.5.0 and later)
reads any geometry that 'wk' handles, shares coincident vertices, and uses
cdtr for the constrained triangulation behind `tri_overlay()` and
`tri_overlay_relate()`. The output of `cdt_pslg()` goes straight into
`wkpool::new_wkpool_tri()`, as shown in
`vignette("wkpool", package = "cdtr")`. The
[polymer](https://github.com/hypertidy/polymer) package builds many-layer
polygon overlay on both.

## What this is for

`cdtr` is the builds-anywhere, permissively licensed baseline of the hypertidy
meshing stack, and the triangulation behind its polygon overlay tools. It has
value on its own: what it adds to a triangulation is information about how the
mesh relates to its input, namely region depth, vertex origin, the input
segments behind every constraint edge, and per-feature winding.

It shares a vertices, segments and triangles contract with other backends, so
which one to use is a choice and not a rewrite. RTriangle (Shewchuk's Triangle)
is the established one in R, and `cdt_pslg()` accepts its `pslg` input as it
is. [laridae](https://github.com/hypertidy/laridae) provides CGAL's
constrained triangulations and meshing, as a persistent mesh that can be edited
and refined. Having more than one option opens up more of what can be done
with triangulation in R.

The `inst/benchmarks/` scripts compare cdtr and RTriangle on North Carolina's
counties and anglr's Tasmanian cadastre, which are polygons, and its Tasmanian
contours, which are open lines and are meshed over their convex hull (the
scripts need anglr, which is no longer on CRAN). Constrained-only, the two give
meshes of the same size, with the same largest area and smallest angle, on all
three. With `max_area` both meet the target on the polygons. Over the hull of
the contours cdtr leaves 0.3% of triangles above it, and reports them in
`unrefined` as `circumcenterOutside`. cdtr adds more Steiner vertices (on the
contours, 5,835 against 5,343 vertices in total), because it protects the
constraints (see above), and reports in `unrefined` where it declined to refine.
Its smallest angles are better on the counties but equally poor on the
contours. Triangle is faster: about three times on the counties with
refinement, and about one and a half times on the cadastre without (the timings
in `bench.R`, on one machine), so it is the better choice if speed on a large
problem matters more than the extra features.
